clue.text: Bit of promotion admitted by TV show judge

indicators.note: something admitted by another is let inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: QI is the BBC quiz show hosted first by Stephen Fry
an ad, an advertisement, is a piece of promotion

explanation.surface: A snippet of advertising slips into a panel show and a judge lets it through.
explanation.definitionFit: A qadi is a judge in a sharia court, a Muslim magistrate.

clue.text: US version of Money for Nothing?

definitions.meaning: in American slang ... means money, as in 'make some ...'
in American slang ... also means nothing at all, as in 'you don't know ...'

explanation.surface: A wink at the Dire Straits song title, imagined in an American rewrite.
explanation.definitionFit: American slang uses the same short word both for cash and, from a ruder longer phrase, for zilch.

clue.text: Rolls up duplicated content? I might

indicators.note: rolls means the word up is turned over, so read from its end back to its start

parts.note: duplicated stands for a doubled R, recalling the twin-R badge of Rolls-Royce named just before

explanation.surface: A query about copied material bundled into rolls, answered by someone saying they might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' turns 'up' into PU. The definition is a cat speaking: if contented, it might do this.
explanation.definitionFit: A contented cat makes a low vibrating hum, so the clue's speaker is the cat saying what it might do when happy.

clue.text: Having set up wireless connection, reach airmen in difficulties, some singing from The Roof

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the word is written upwards, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: wi-fi is a wireless network connection

indicators.note: letters in difficulties are thrown into disorder and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: After getting online, someone contacts airmen in trouble, with a snatch of song thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses WIFI to IFIW; 'in difficulties' rearranges REACHAIRMEN to EREARICHMAN. The Roof is Fiddler on the Roof, the musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Tevye's famous number in the musical Fiddler on the Roof is this song, so it is some singing from that show.

clue.text: Performer didn't at first catch ID of soldier from the back

indicators.note: reading from the back means the whole string of letters is taken from its end to its start
at first points to the opening letter of the word didn't

parts.note: to nab is to catch or seize
a soldier identifies himself by name and number, NO being the usual abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A performer at first fails to get a soldier's identity, viewed from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' takes D from 'didn't'; joined to NAB and NAME + NO it makes DNABNAMENO, which 'from the back' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A busker playing several instruments at once is a solo entertainer, a kind of performer.

clue.text: Reduced selection with California holiday package? FIND ME A BAR!!

indicators.note: a package wraps its contents, so the shortened word goes round the others
reduced means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a choice is a selection
CA is the postal abbreviation for California
HOL is a common short form of holiday

explanation.surface: A cut-down range of Californian holiday packages, with a desperate cry for a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' drops the last letter, giving CHOIC. The capitalised cry is a chocolate addict wanting a bar of chocolate, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone addicted to chocolate would demand a bar of it, so the cry characterises such a person.

clue.text: Something sloppy about order to hang loose

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: goo is a sticky, sloppy substance
a command is an order

explanation.surface: A messy business surrounding a command to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is slang for wearing no underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase means wearing no underpants, so everything is left to dangle freely, a cheeky reading of the idiom.

clue.text: Poor mite knocked back jelly and cake

indicators.note: knocked back suggests something turned round, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: agar is a jelly made from seaweed
a muffin is a small cake

explanation.surface: A poor child gulps down jelly and cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' looks like gulping food but reverses AGAR to RAGA.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragged, dirty child is pitied as a poor little scruff, so the phrase describes one.

clue.text: I'm surprised to get approval for trap

parts.note: ho is an exclamation of surprise
OK signals approval

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished to find their snare approved.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch a fish or ensnare someone is to trap them, and a barbed catch device does just that.

clue.text: Do/die strategy oddly works to thwart flipping Italian Job fleet

indicators.note: thwart here means lying across, so the shuffled letters are set across the middle of the other word
flipping means turning over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the getaway cars in the film The Italian Job were Minis

indicators.note: oddly suggests the letters are behaving strangely, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A plan to stop the getaway cars in The Italian Job heist, all or nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' reverses MINIS to SINIM; 'oddly' rearranges WORKS to KORSW, which 'to thwart' places across the middle. 'oddly' looks like a take-odd-letters signal; it is the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a situation where you either succeed by your own efforts or fail completely, an all-or-nothing approach.

clue.text: It was a mistake losing top jobs in the theatre

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, which is dropped

parts.note: oops is what you say when you've made a mistake

explanation.surface: An apology over a slip, with someone losing top jobs on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the theatre' is the operating theatre, not the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgical operations are informally called by a short form, and they are performed in an operating theatre.

clue.text: Manx dog looking around box of chickens

indicators.note: looking around suggests turning back, so the shortened word is reversed
a Manx cat has no tail, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: pooch is informal for a dog

explanation.surface: A tailless dog sniffs round the hen house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manx' cuts POOCH to POOC; 'looking around' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen house or cage for poultry is a pen for keeping hens.

clue.text: In consequence, not in range

indicators.note: not means the following word is left out of the longer one

parts.note: again can mean in return or as a result, an older sense
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something follows as a result, but not within reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not in' removes IN from AGAIN. An AGA is a British brand of heavy cast-iron kitchen stove.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a large kitchen cooker, and the Aga is the best-known make of one.

clue.text: Enforce restriction against Beaverbrook?

parts.note: to press something is to force or insist on it
a bar is a restriction or prohibition
on can mean against, as in leaning on a wall

explanation.surface: A call to impose a ban on a famous newspaper owner.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Beaverbrook owned the Daily Express; the question mark marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Beaverbrook was a powerful newspaper proprietor, an example of a mogul of the printed news.

clue.text: Bus in collision with truck towing alien one, hardly roadworthy

definitions.note: an adjective phrase defining a noun: an old car in this state

indicators.note: towing puts the alien behind, at the end of the other letters
vehicles in collision are crumpled, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: ET is the alien in Spielberg's film

explanation.surface: A bus crashes into a lorry that is hauling an alien, leaving a wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in collision' rearranges BUSTRUCK to RUSTBUCK; 'towing' puts the alien at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a decrepit, corroded old car, one that is barely fit to drive.

clue.text: Playfully ragged Sanchez about forward's third celebration

indicators.note: about means going round, so the rearranged name surrounds a letter
ragged means torn about, so the name's letters are rearranged
third points to the third letter of the word forward's

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: Footballer Sanchez is teased about a forward's goal celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ragged' rearranges the name to SCHEZAN, which 'about' wraps round R, the third letter of 'forward's'. The answer is a musical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical term directs a passage to be played in a light, joking, sportive manner.

clue.text: Yen for the poorer areas and the activity of the sewer?

indicators.note: for here links the longing to the place it is directed at, the place coming first

parts.note: back streets are the poorer parts of town, with street shortened to ST
a yen is an itch, a longing

explanation.surface: A craving for the slums, and something about the sewers below them.
explanation.walkthrough: The sewer is one who sews, not a drain.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong overlapping stitch is a seamstress's technique, so it is what someone who sews does.

clue.text: In goal

definitions.meaning: being in means being at your house, not out
in games, the target or base a player aims to reach is called this

explanation.surface: Two words, as terse as a sports result.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying in means being at one's residence, and in some games the base or target is also called by this word.

clue.text: IQ = 4 x 2?

parts.note: a four-by-two is a length of timber, so an intelligence equal to it suggests a very stupid person

explanation.surface: An equation giving someone's intelligence as a timber measurement.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone very stupid, comparing them to a dense piece of wood.

clue.text: What the Romans found when they came north across the Border? Yes and no

definitions.text: What the Romans found when they came north

indicators.note: across signals letters spanning the gap between two words, taken from inside them

explanation.surface: Roman legions marching north over the Border, a yes-and-no matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yes and no' admits the Romans found York but never truly crossed into Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Eboracum was the Roman name for York, shortened in Latin abbreviations, a city the Romans founded in the north.

clue.text: PR "icon" somehow joining dots up

indicators.note: somehow means the letters come together in some unstated arrangement

explanation.surface: A public relations star connecting the dots to make a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges PR, ICON and DOTS; the whole clue also describes a press manipulator joining dots to make a story.
explanation.definitionFit: A media adviser who puts a favourable slant on events is a PR figure who joins the dots for the public.

clue.text: Old, swinging, Sash

parts.note: swinging both ways means bisexual, shortened to bi

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned, swaying sash window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sash' looks like a window but is a Japanese garment.
explanation.definitionFit: The broad sash tied round a kimono is a Japanese waistband.

clue.text: It makes for zero sex appeal

definitions.text: It makes for zero sex appeal

parts.note: Z is a symbol for zero in some notations
it is an old term for sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'

explanation.surface: Something that ruins your attractiveness altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimple on the face is notoriously unattractive, so it kills allure entirely.

clue.text: Acting chairman tables agenda to begin proceedings

indicators.note: to begin points to the opening letter of each of the preceding words

explanation.surface: A stand-in chair puts the agenda on the table to start the meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for things done, the word means the recorded transactions or minutes of a society.

clue.text: Will I get nothing, assuming Lord has young child?

definitions.text: Will I get nothing, assuming Lord has young child?

indicators.note: assuming means taking on, so the word for nothing takes the other letters inside

parts.note: nix is slang for nothing

indicators.note: has means holds, so the lord's title holds the child inside

parts.note: Herr is German for lord or master
a baby is often called it

explanation.surface: A daughter worries she'll be left nothing in the will now his lordship has a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: Herr is German for lord; a baby is 'it'. The whole clue is the worried daughter's question.
explanation.definitionFit: A female heir is the one hoping to get something under a will, so her worry fits.

clue.text: When Open University let slip how old we are inspired frenzy

indicators.note: let slip means letting something drop away, so those letters are removed

parts.note: 'our age' is how old we are
OU is the abbreviation for the Open University, a British distance-learning university

explanation.surface: A university blurts out our age, and someone flies into a fury.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetic fury or passionate enthusiasm is an old literary sense of extreme anger.

clue.text: You shouldn't have repeated for so long …

indicators.note: repeated means the short word is said twice in succession

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks, said on receiving a gift

explanation.surface: Thanking someone over and over for so long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so long' looks like a duration, but it is a goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal goodbye, like cheerio, is a way of saying farewell.

clue.text: … or not so long, Celtic island king under attack?

definitions.meaning: a small measure of length, a twelfth of a foot
in Scotland and Ireland, a small island is called this, from Gaelic innis
a king under attack in chess is in check

explanation.surface: A Celtic island where a king faces attack.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues the previous one: 'so long' there means goodbye, 'not so long' here means short.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of twelve to a foot is a short length, a Gaelic word means islet, and the chess phrase is abbreviated the same.

clue.text: Make one's way to the old Theatreland

definitions.meaning: to ... is to go or travel, as in ... one's way
..., the West End of London, the traditional theatre district

explanation.surface: Someone heads off to the theatre district of yesteryear.
explanation.definitionFit: Wending means travelling slowly or by an indirect route, going somewhere.

clue.text: Embark on new diet, so select a different course?

definitions.meaning: tack is old slang for food, as in hardtack, so changing it is changing diet
to change direction when sailing or in policy

explanation.surface: Starting a diet means choosing a new course at dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Altering a sailing direction, or a policy, is the idiom; food slang gives the joke.
